newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: INTERVIEW - Bombardier prospects Asian jet market.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Bombardier prospects Asian jet market.

text.p: Bombardier Inc saw a big market for its range of corporate and regional jets in Asia but lack of infrastructure in the region may limit sales at present, Vice-Chairman J.R. Andre Bombardier said on Wednesday.

"There is a big market in the area but the infrastucture has to be developed ... In most Asian countries, they have to develop that aspect," Bombardier said of the absence of sufficient airports on the continent.
"Right now what we are trying to do is to show them, to demonstrate the benefits of the product to them," he told Reuters of his company's efforts at selling corporate and regional jets in Asia.
Bombardier declined to give projections on the company's profits for 1996-97 ending January 31. "All I can say is we will have more profits and sales," he said.
He said 1995-96 profits were at about C$300 million dollars "but we had to take a write down on one of our projects, so it went down to C$150 million".
Bombardier is in Manila as part of a Canadian business delegation on a three-nation Asian tour that also covers South Korea and Thailand.

"It is going to take time. You have to sell one (corporate jet) to one of them and when it demonstrates that it is efficient for them ... like in America where most of the big business are using jets to improve their operations," he said.

Bombardier is a conglomerate that also makes motorised consumer products such as snowmobiles and personal watercraft, and rail transportation equipment, including shuttle-train cars for the Channel tunnel, and missile systems. It has announced plans to make a neighbourhood electric vehicle.

Since it bought Canadair from the Canadian government in the early 1980s, it has expanded its reach in the aerospace sector by producing a regional jet, purchasing Belfast-based Short Brothers, and buying turboprop plane maker de Havilland. Bombardier also owns Learjet Inc.
Bombardier said the company's latest corporate jet, the Global Express which can fly non-stop for 6,700 nautical miles (12,408 km), was expected to give it a big advantage.
"Our advantage over our competitors is our new product, Global Express," he said, adding that the firm had so far received 55 orders for the plane.
"Worldwide, the total market potential for Global Express or that type of aircraft is 800 units. The yearly market for that type of aircraft is 100 to 150," he said.
He said the jet, now undergoing flight tests, was awaiting clearance from the U.S. Federal Aviation Authority and was expected to hit the market next year.

Bombardier said the company's target market for the business jet, powered by engines developed by Rolls Royce Plc in joint venture with BMW, was "governments and international companies who want to go around the globe."
Bombardier said on his current Asian tour, he had also prospected the market for the company's highly successful 50-seat Canadair Regional jet.
In the Philippines, an archipelago of 7,100 islands, there could be good prospects for the company's amphibious craft, he said.

Another possibility was to sell train cars for Manila's light rail transit system, he said, adding that Bombardier had bought the European company that had supplied train cars to the Philippines several years ago.
